item.title: Types of Thought Distortions and How to Change Your Thinking
item.description:
Thought distortions are patterns of thinking that don’t match reality. Also known as cognitive distortions, they are automatic, inaccurate, often irrational thoughts and beliefs that have little or no evidence to back them up, and that color the way you view yourself, others, and the world, and shape your experiences and behavior.

Types of Thought Distortions

Mental Filtering Mental filtering is zooming in on one negative detail of an experience, frequently taken out of context, while disregarding the broader picture and ignoring everything else about it that is good, positive, or neutral. You do well at school, for instance, but keep beating yourself up and calling yourself stupid because of one question you answered wrong on a test.

Catastrophizing Catastrophizing is when you blow things out of proportion, interpret even harmless situations as frightening, and anticipate the worst, despite having no evidence that such an outcome is possible or even likely. For example, thinking “My son has not called; he must have been in a car accident,” or “This spot on my skin is probably skin cancer.”

Emotional Reasoning Emotional reasoning undermines your logical processes and assumes that what you feel about a situation reflects its reality, regardless of the facts or any evidence to the contrary. For example, “I’m feeling anxious, so something bad must be about to happen,” or “I’m feeling guilty, so I must have done something wrong.

All-Or-Nothing Thinking All-or-nothing thinking is seeing everything in terms of black or white, with no middle ground or shades of gray. Everything is either one extreme or the other, totally perfect or completely bad. A single mistake, for instance, is seen as ruining an entire project, or anything less than an A+ as a failure.

Should Statements “Should” statements are rigid, unrealistic rules you create for yourself using words such as “should,” “should not,” and “must,” that put a lot of pressure on you and lead to guilt and the feeling that you are never enough. “I must make sure the house is spotless before company comes,” for instance, or “I should always know the right thing to say.”

Magnification and Minimization Magnification and minimization are two sides of the same coin. Magnification highlights negatives, exaggerating them and making them seem larger than they are, such as thinking, “I made a mistake at work, so now my whole career is ruined.”

Minimization, on the other hand, diminishes strengths and achievements, making them seem small and insignificant. It can also trivialize important realities, such as ignoring a persistent problem in a relationship and saying, “Everything’s fine, they’re just overreacting.”

Dismissing the Positive Dismissing the positive is discounting the good things that happen to you as not counting, being unimportant or invalid, or chalking them up to luck or coincidence by using disqualifying statements such as, “It was just a lucky guess,” when commended for giving a good answer on a test, or “The only reason I got hired for the job was because the interviewer was desperate to find someone to fill the position.”

Jumping to Conclusions Jumping to conclusions is assuming that something is true or likely to happen, without any evidence to support it. Thinking a friend is angry with you because he is not smiling, for instance, or predicting an outcome there is no basis for, such as “the doctor is going to tell me I have cancer,” when you are on your way for a routine checkup.

Labeling Labeling is judging and defining yourself or someone else negatively, based on an isolated incident or behavior, such as calling yourself an idiot, loser, or failure, because you made a small mistake at work, or calling someone else a jerk, because they accidentally bumped into you.

Overgeneralization Overgeneralization is assuming that one negative event means that all future events will also have negative outcomes and stretching a bad moment into a permanent cycle of defeat, making sweeping assumptions such as, “I misplaced my keys. I can never keep track of anything,” or “I got stuck in traffic this morning. I’ll always be late for work.”

Personalization Personalization is feeling guilty about and blaming yourself for problems that are not your fault, and imagining you caused them even when you had nothing to do with them, or they were issues that were out of your control. Thinking “It’s my fault our team lost the game,” for instance, or “It’s my fault my friend is not enjoying this party.”

Comparisons Comparisons involve comparing yourself or your performance to someone else’s and magnifying your faults and weaknesses while emphasizing their strengths, even when you don’t know all the facts, and then feeling inadequate or inferior and thinking thoughts such as, “All my friends are doing better than I am,” for instance.

Effects of Thought Distortions

Adding to or subtracting from what’s really happening can cloud your judgment, increase stress, and have a detrimental impact on many areas of your life. Catastrophizing over a financial situation or a benign health symptom, for instance, can disrupt your sleep or lead to panic attacks.

Being convinced you’re a failure or that nobody likes you can cause you to isolate and avoid social situations or keep from pursuing new opportunities at work. All-or-nothing thinking and emotional reasoning can lead you to see threats all around you where none exist.

Although everyone tends to have negative thoughts once in a while, if they are constant, they are likely to turn into strongly held beliefs. Left unchecked, a steady flow of negative expectations and predictions can erode your self-esteem, cause you to see yourself as not good enough or unable to change, and lead to frustration, depression, and anxiety.

Causes of Distorted Thinking

In some cases, thought distortions are the brain’s way of looking for mental shortcuts to avoid having to process a lot of information at the same time. Instead of having to deal with future uncertainty, for instance, you make a habit of assuming the worst.

In other cases, distorted thoughts may be your mind’s way of looking for solutions to potential future events, such as the breakup of a relationship or a failing grade at school.

While there is no conclusive evidence of a definitive cause for them, distorted thoughts seem more likely to emerge in times of high stress, and some studies have indicated that people who experience adverse events in childhood, such as financial hardship, abandonment, chronic illness, or trauma, are more vulnerable to distorted thinking as adults.

Tips for Putting an End to Thought Distortions

Identify your thought distortions Becoming aware of and identifying the thought distortions you are most prone to is the first, most important step. It is what enables you to deconstruct them and reframe them in a more positive and realistic way.

Practice nonjudgmental awareness Practice acknowledging your thoughts without judging them or beating yourself up about them.

Question your automatic thoughts Take a closer look at your negative thoughts and ask yourself how rational or realistic they are, if there is any evidence to support them, and if you might be overlooking something positive.

Keep a gratitude journal Look for things you can be thankful for and focus on what is going well in your life without downplaying it. End your day by writing three positive things in your journal that you accomplished or experienced, no matter how small they may seem.

Consider therapy A trained mental health professional can help you identify and address your thought distortions, equip you with tools to reframe and replace them, and help you think in a more balanced way.

If you need more help than this article on thought distortions can provide, and would like to set up a risk-free appointment with one of the faith-based counselors at our location, please give our reception team a call.

item.title: Christian Premarital Counseling: The Framework for Life’s Storms
item.description:
Oh, the naivety of young love. If you’ve been married for a while, this article is not for you. You already know the pitfalls that can come when two become one. You already know, probably firsthand, the challenges that newly married couples face, even those who think that love conquers all. According to John 15:13, “Greater love has no one than this: to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.”  But if you’re considering marriage or are already engaged, then please continue to read. Please. For the sake of your marriage and your future and your love and your romantic partner and your family. Please continue to read about the benefits of Christian premarital counseling.

Does Love Conquer All?

No. It most certainly does not. At least not in the way you think it does. God’s love does conquer all. His love restored human communion with the Creator of the universe and saved us all from eternal damnation.  But does your romantic love have the ability to transcend time, change outcomes, and restore all things? Not so much.

Your love for your partner, as pure and intense and selfless as it may seem, does not conquer all the pitfalls you will face during your marriage. Human love, while it is a beautiful, powerful thing, is still fallible, just like the people experiencing it. Love is a good start. It’s a great foundation. It’s even what motivates you to pursue a deeper connection with each other, but it has its limitations.

Assuming that all the obstacles of marriage will be solved by the love you share is naïve. Love will give you the motivation to try to find a solution to your issues, but it will not give you the tools.

You Need Tools: Benefits of Christian Premarital Counseling

You wouldn’t build a house without the right equipment, a blueprint, and some experts in the field. When you get married, you are building a house of sorts. Not a physical building, of course, but the house where your life story will live. Where your heart dwells and where your future will thrive or die.

When you build a house, the most important, fundamental part is the foundation. And as an engaged (or potentially engaged) couple, you need to build a solid, unshakable foundation on which to build the house of your marriage.

Christian premarital counseling gives you the tools to build that firm foundation. It shows you effective ways to communicate with each other and helps you understand your and your partner’s expectations. The costs of happiness in most relationships are attributed to broken communication and financial stress and strain. Having such a framework helps you frame whether these expectations are reasonable, biblical, and healthy.

Your counselor will help you talk about sensitive topics like physical intimacy, past relationships, integration of families, financial issues, and future plans without letting tension erode the relationship.

The Practical Skills You’ll Learn

Some people think that premarital counseling is just a designated place to talk about problems in the relationship. But the reality is that it goes way beyond that by giving you the methodology to solve them. You’ll learn skills for identifying your negative interaction cycle, such as pursue and withdraw, how to use “I Statements” effectively, and a guide to structured problem-solving that helps to keep emotional reactions in check.

Discovering new and interesting things about your partner is what keeps the spark lit. Through premarital counseling, you will learn how to maintain curiosity about your partner. While becoming “comfortable” with each other is often the goal because it can bring peace, the unfortunate flip side to that story is that it can also lead to boredom if curiosity isn’t maintained.

That’s why it’s important to continue to see your partner as an evolving person with new ideas, dreams, and challenges. Premarital counseling equips you with techniques to continuously ask intentional, open-ended questions to keep the interest and intrigue alive and help keep the fires burning.

Expectations Vs. Reality

Everyone has their vision of ideal love. As a child, you might read fairy tales about a prince and a charming maiden who live “happily ever after.” But that expectation is rooted in fantasy, not reality. The reality is that even people in the healthiest relationships who carry unspoken expectations are setting themselves and their intended up for disaster.

What a “good spouse” does, how holidays should work, how often you see family, how affection is shown, who handles what at home… the list goes on and on. Most people don’t even know that they have these subtle and hidden expectations until they’re not met because they’re often wrapped in their memories and experiences.

Much of what you learn to be “absolute truths” and relational structures is established in your childhood. How did your dad treat your mom? Did your parental figures act romantic toward each other, or did they live as roommates? How were chores divided? By traditional gender roles?

Premarital counseling helps you drag those hidden expectations out into the light. You’ll talk about your expectations surrounding communication, conflict (and resolution), chores, faith, money, emotional needs, and even how each of you defines respect. Even when you know what your partner expects, meeting those expectations can be difficult. But if you at least understand each other better, you can strive toward meeting or negotiating them.

Preparing for Life’s Storms with Christian Premarital Counseling in Washington

Every couple walks into their engagement with excitement, hope, and a few stars in their eyes. And that optimism is a beautiful thing because God did design love to be joyful. But life, even really good lives, isn’t immune to pitfalls and obstacles. Eventually, illness, financial strain, job loss, grief, infertility, parenting challenges, spiritual drought, or just the stresses and exhaustion of everyday life can shake even the strongest couples.

Christian premarital counseling in Washington state gives you the chance to talk honestly about how you each handle stress, disappointment, and fear before you’re standing in the thick of it. You’ll learn how to support each other during hardship without shutting down or getting angry, blaming, or withdrawing. You’ll learn how to lean on each other instead of letting these things pull you apart.

Dealing With Others

When you’re in love, it feels like you and your spouse are on your own little continent, where the whole world fades into the background, and it seems like nothing and no one else matters. But that’s not reality. Marriage doesn’t happen in a vacuum. As wonderful as that “just us” bubble feels now, real life will eventually burst it.

You will interact with people of the opposite sex. So will your partner. Premarital counseling will help you decide on boundaries with the opposite sex now, while you’re still in the “honeymoon phase.” You will learn how to handle these relationships with transparency and in ways that meet each other’s needs and help you and your partner feel secure.

You will also learn how to handle relationships with in-laws, coworkers, friends, church members, neighbors, and people your spouse knew long before they knew you, because all of these connections, healthy and complicated, will influence your marriage in some way.

You Need God

God wants to help you have a successful marriage.

God is the author of love, even romantic love. He created Eve as a special gift to Adam. The Bible is full of stories of commitment and covenant. Christ’s sacrificial and selfless love for the church is the ultimate template for how a husband is to love his wife (Ephesians 5).

Chrisitan premarital counseling can be part of God’s plan to help your future marriage succeed. In Proverbs, it says, “Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22 NIV). And that’s really the heart of premarital counseling. That’s really the heart of God.

You don’t have to walk blindly and figure life out on your own. God wants to walk with you into this big life-changing thing called marriage. And to that end, He has placed resources around you, tools, such as counselors, mentors, and of course, the Bible. He has offered His Holy Spirit as a guide. You just have to choose to accept the help and the wisdom He has made available to you.

What To Do When Love Doesn’t Conquer All

You need to acknowledge that your human love, as beautiful and intense as it is, is insufficient by itself. You need to willingly bring outside wisdom, both human (counseling) and divine (Scripture and the Holy Spirit), into your union before the crisis hits.

When you make the conscious decision to pursue premarital counseling, you are honoring God by seeking the “many advisers” He promised would lead to success. You’re committing to building your house not just on good feelings and mutual interests, but on the Solid Rock of eternal wisdom and covenant love.

Contact us today to schedule a Christian premarital counseling appointment with a Christian counselor in Washington state who can help you begin your marriage on a strong foundation.

item.title: Beyond Guilt and Shame: Christian Counseling for Externally Oriented Struggles
item.description:
Have you ever found yourself standing in the middle of your closet, surrounded by clothes with price tags still attached? Maybe you find yourself scrolling through social media and comparing your home to what you see in the photos. Materialism isn’t as simple as wanting nice things; consequently, the pursuit of material things often becomes a prison of guilt and shame. This prison is not how God designed us to live.

But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you – Matthew 6:33, ESV

Many Christians today struggle with the weight of materialism that previous generations had never encountered. Our culture today screams from every direction about how our worth is measured by what we own or don’t own.

From what we wear to the house we live in, we are under a constant barrage of temptations to compare. This message seeps into our thoughts and creates a battlefield between what we know is not true and what the world says is important.

The Spiritual Trap of Materialism

We often think of materialism in terms of someone greedy or obsessed with wealth. The truth is that materialism is much more subtle, especially for Christians, who seek to follow God’s heart.

Materialism isn’t just about having nice things. It is where we place our security, our hope, and our identity. It is how we often measure success in today’s world. This is how material possessions begin to fill spaces that were designed for God to occupy.

We don’t need to live in shame or feel guilty about the blessings that He gives to us. Scripture tells us that every good and perfect gift comes from Him. It is not in receiving these gifts that we become entangled in materialism, but rather when we make those gifts our god. When we place our happiness and security in what we can buy and acquire or display, we have shifted from spiritual to worldly living.

Once we are entangled in this, it becomes a vicious cycle. We find ways to convince ourselves that we need the things we see. And in that justification, we acquire it and feel satisfied for a fleeting moment. Then we become overwhelmed with guilt, asking ourselves, “Did I need this? Could the money have been spent better? What will people think?” That’s followed by the shame when we hear, “You’re not a good steward. “You’re selfish.”

Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. – Matthew 6:19-21, ESV

The Pattern of Guilt and Shame in Material Pursuit

To overcome the cycle associated with material pursuit, it is important to understand the difference between guilt and shame. We feel guilty about our purchasing desires or inability to be content. We then compare ourselves to others who seem to have less and feel guilty for wanting more.

This thought process leads us to look at credit card statements and feel guilty about our choices. Yet underneath all the guilt, shame is at work, whispering destructive lies about who we are.

Shame, on the other hand, tells us we’re greedy when we are simply human. Shame tells us we’re bad stewards when we are learning to navigate a chaotic and complex world. It then tells us we are failures as Christians because we struggle with contentment.

These thoughts trap us in a cycle and can lead to other issues, such as emotional issues, eating, shopping binges, and isolation.

Spiritually, the impact of guilt and shame cannot be understated. As we constantly battle these emotions, we find it harder to pray, read scripture, and believe that God delights in us. This leads to avoiding fellowship because we fear others will see through our disguise to the real image.

We may even stop tithing or giving because we are too guilty about our spending. This is where we find that the very relationship that could set us free has become clouded by the shame and guilt that we carry.

There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus – Romans 8:1, ESV

God Desires for Us to Be Free from Condemnation

God’s heart toward us is not one of disappointment regarding our struggle with materialism. He does not want to see us bound by guilt and shame. He is not sitting in judgment of a credit card statement or an Amazon cart. What He does see are His children, whom He adores, who are learning to navigate a world that consistently pulls them away from Him.

The difference between conviction and condemnation plays a crucial role in freedom from materialism. Conviction is when the Holy Spirit gently nudges and redirects us toward God’s desired plans for us. Condemnation is the harsh voice of the enemy that beats us down and leads us into hiding from God. Condemnation drives us away, but conviction draws us to God.

When we are feeling convicted about materialism, it is not to shame us; it is meant to set us free. God knows that when our hearts are tangled up in the pursuit of things, we miss out on His joy and peace.

He is not angry with the struggle we have, and He doesn’t show disappointment. He desires to see us walk in freedom from the vicious bondage of materialism. It is His love that compels Him to bring correction that will make changes in our lives.

God wants to provide not only our needs, but He also wants to bless us in abundance. It’s not that He doesn’t want us to have nice things. It’s that He wants us to have an identity in Him rather than belongings. When we are anchored in His love for us, we receive blessings with gratitude and hold them lightly because we know that our treasure is in heaven and not in the world.

The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing. – Zephaniah 3:17, ESV

How Christian Counseling Provides a Healing Pathway

Anyone struggling with guilt and shame from materialistic patterns does not have to carry the burden alone. Christian Counseling can offer a path to healing that addresses not just the symptoms but the root causes of the struggle.

Secular counseling often focuses on behavior modification, but biblical counseling will recognize that material struggles are often symptoms of deeper emotional needs.

A Christian counselor can help with identifying the lies about worth, security, and identity that have been believed. Using Scripture, these counselors can guide us to discover God’s truth about our identity and how God sees us.

Using a faith-based plan, Christian counselors can help develop practical strategies for managing the triggers and making wise financial decisions. This will lead to contentment in building a relationship with God.

Some practical steps that may be included in faith-based Christian Counseling are:

  • Learning to pause before purchasing and ask God about the purchase.
  • Developing gratitude to shift focus from what you lack to your blessings.
  • Create accountability and relationships with other believers,
  • Establish financial boundaries that reflect values rather than impulses.

The goal of overcoming guilt and shame from materialism isn’t for us to live in deprivation. The main goal is freedom to make decisions from a place of peace rather than compulsion. This freedom allows us to enjoy God’s blessings without guilt and shame because we know our security is from Him.

Living in Freedom

God understands we live in a world where success is measured by one’s belongings. This is not how he intended for us to live. God’s plan has always included freedom and blessings of abundance. The mentality of guilt and shame comes from an enemy who wants to see us bound.

If you or someone you know is trapped in patterns of guilt and shame involving materialism, reach out to a local Christian counselor. Freedom can become a part of everyday life, replacing the shackles of guilt and shame.
